newsitem.title: USA: American General $665 mln deal seen as good move.
newsitem.headline: American General $665 mln deal seen as good move.

text.p: American General Corp's agreement on Monday to buy Home Beneficial Corp is a smart move for a company determined to grow its business in the tough "home service" segment of life insurance, analysts said.

The Houston-based American General and Virginia-based Home Beneficial jointly announced a definitive agreement under which American General will acquire Home Beneficial for a total of $665 million or $39 a share.
Home Beneficial shares climbed 8-1/2 to 37-3/4 in midafternoon trading, while American General eased 3/8 to 39-7/8.

The deal, expected to close at the end of March 1997, reflects the ongoing consolidation among life insurers, particularly those in "home service" -- a low-premium segment including benefits for burial, focused on lower-middle-class families, analysts said.
"It's a very good strategic fit for American General's home service operation," said Michael Albanese, vice president of A.M. Best Co.
"Strategically, it helps American General maintain their position in what otherwise is a slow-growth sector of the market."
New-business growth for home service companies has been in the low single digits at best, and in many cases is on the decline, said Albanese.

"The home-service market is an expensive-type business because it has small policies, small face amounts and small premiums," said Larry Mayewski, senior vice president of A.M. Best's life/health division.
The average size of a policy is only $5,000, and expenses are usually high because agents have traditionally gone door-to-door to collect premiums.
"American General recognizes that it's a very difficult market to grow, and one way to grow is through acquisition," said Mayewski.

Home Beneficial is also a good geographic fit for American General, since the former is strong in the mid-Atlantic region while the latter's customer base is in the South and Southwest, said Albanese.
The deal is American General's third life insurance company acquisition in the past two years, for a total cost of $2.2 billion.

"Through the combination of these two companies, we believe we can achieve economies of scale resulting in annual expense savings of $20 million," said Robert Devlin, president and chief executive of American General, in a statement earlier on Monday.
American General is among the nation's five biggest life insurers on the basis of sales.
Another analyst said the deal looked good for American General's shareholders, but that the company's return on equity of only eight percent in the home-service area was slightly disturbing.
"The home-service business at American General is over-capitalized in order to maintain its AAA claims-paying rating," said Caitlin Long, analyst at Salomon Brothers.
"Even though the move is good from the perspective of gaining economies of scale, it's still a low-return business within American General's corporate structure," she said.
But Long said she would nonetheless increase her American General earnings estimate by five cents to $3.55 in 1997 and $3.95 in 1998. --Hartford newsroom (860) 727-0224
